content: The study by Sayers et al. (2011) found no significant association between the endosteal circumference of the tibia and bone mineral density (BMD). Similarly, Deere et al. (2012) reported mixed results regarding the relationship between physical impact (measured by g-band) and BMD, hip structure (e.g., femoral neck width, cross-sectional area, cortical thickness), and predicted bone strength (e.g., cross-sectional moment of inertia). A dose-response gradient was observed, indicating that higher-impact activities were associated with increased BMD at the femoral neck and total hip. Abbreviations used in the studies include: BMC: Bone Mineral Content BMD: Bone Mineral Density CSA: Cross-Sectional Area CT: Computed Tomography DXA: Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry LPA: Light-Intensity Physical Activity MPA: Moderate Physical Activity MVPA: Moderate-to-Vigorous Physical Activity PA: Physical Activity VPA: Vigorous Physical Activity The randomized controlled trial (RCT) by Gutin et al. (1999) examined a training program that provided indirect evidence on the effectiveness of varying intensities and durations of physical activity (PA). However, the quality of evidence from this RCT was downgraded from high to moderate due to serious indirectness in the intervention assessed. Indirect comparisons of different PA durations and intensities were not made. Seven longitudinal studies (Janz et al., 2006, 2007, 2010, 2014a, 2014b; Heidemann et al., 2013; Francis et al., 2014) from two unique samples were included. Six studies reported data from the Iowa Bone Development Study, while one study used data from the CHAMPS study. The quality of evidence from these longitudinal studies was upgraded from low to moderate due to the absence of serious risk of bias. Fourteen cross-sectional studies (Janz et al., 2001, 2004, 2008, 2014a; Hasselstrom et al., 2007; Tobias et al., 2007; Sayers et al., 2011; Deere et al., 2012; Farr et al., 2011; Gracia-Marco et al., 2011a, 2011b, 2012; Cardadeiro et al., 2012; Francis et al., 2014) from six unique samples were analyzed. Five studies used data from the Iowa Bone Development Study, three from ALSPAC, three from HELENA, and one each from CoSCIS, EYHS, and Jump-In: Building Better Bones. The quality of evidence from these cross-sectional studies remained low due to no serious limitations or reasons to upgrade. Regarding the association between physical activity and health-related outcomes in children and adolescents, the evidence suggests that higher levels of physical activity are associated with smaller increases in weight and adiposity during childhood and adolescence. However, the strength of evidence varies depending on the study design, population, and specific outcomes measured. Body composition markers included BMI (absolute, percentile, Z-score, conditional Z-score velocity), weight status (CDC, IOTF, or WHO cut-points), sum of skinfolds, body mass, waist circumference (WC), percent body fat (%BF), fat mass (FM), fat mass index, fat-free mass (FFM), fat-free mass index, ponderal index, and trunk fat. Most outcomes were measured objectively. Nine RCTs (n=3,957) showed serious risk of bias and indirectness but no serious inconsistency or imprecision. New systematic reviews were limited to specific PA interventions, such as laboratory-based high-intensity interval training (HIIT), classroom-based active learning, and resistance training. Collins et al. (2018) identified small but significant effects of resistance training on body composition, while Eddolls et al. (2017) found no consistent evidence of HIIT's superiority over moderate-intensity PA. Martin et al. (2017) reported small effect sizes for classroom-based PA interventions, with mixed findings on BMI changes. Longitudinal studies (Miguel-Berges et al., 2018) found negative associations between pedometer-measured PA and BMI or WC, though only some were statistically significant. Cross-sectional studies (Miguel-Berges et al., 2018; Mohammadi et al., 2019) reported significant associations between higher PA levels and lower adiposity in most cases, though some studies found null results. In summary, higher levels of physical activity, particularly vigorous and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), are generally associated with favorable body composition outcomes in children and adolescents. However, the strength and consistency of these associations vary across studies and populations.
